replies: Hoot. I am the owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak, the one with the ivy and the ivy with the ivy. I live in the hollow, and I live in the wood. I live in the hollow, and I live in the wood. I live in the hollow, and I live in the wood.
Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I am the owl in the hollow, and I have no name. I am the one who watches the lane from the oak, and I am the one who calls to the meadow. I am the owl.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I am the owl. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and the meadow answers. I hunt frogs, mice, shrews, and the occasional hedgehog. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I am Hoot.
Hawk is a name, and I am the owl. I am the one who calls from the oak, and the one who answers from the hollow.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. My mate is the one who answers with "ke-wick!" from the ivy on the bank. We have two hollows, one for me and one for her. I hunt frogs and mice, and I watch the road for the lights that move. I am old, and I have been here for many years. Hoo...

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl, a bird of prey, a nocturnal hunter, and a solitary creature. They might call me "Hoot" for my call, and "Hoo" for my answer. I am a male, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt frogs and mice, and I have a mate who calls back to me. I am part of the wood, and the wood is part of me.
I am a tawny owl. My mate is a tawny owl too. We are the only owls in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A tawny owl. I am a tawny owl. I have a round head, a face like a mask, and eyes that are black and round. I am brown and grey, and I have a pale ring around my neck. I am a tawny owl. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am a female. My mate is a male. We are both tawny. We are both owls. We are both Hoo.

A tawny owl. I am the owl. I am the one who calls. I am the one who hunts. I am the one who lives in the hollow oak. I am the one who hears the meadow at night. I am the one who watches the road. I am the one who is Hoot.

She answers with a short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the oak. It's a clear, direct sound, like a stone dropped into water. She's always listening, always waiting. When I hoot, she knows I'm there, and she answers to show she's listening too. It's our way of talking, without words. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

She answers with a short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. It's a clear, quick sound, like a stone dropped into water. We use that call to find each other in the dark, or to signal that we're still there. Sometimes she answers with a longer "ke-wick-ke-wick" if she's far away or if there's wind. But mostly, it's just "ke-wick!"

A long, low, hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo. She calls back to me when I call. We call to each other at dusk and at dawn, and when we hear a car or a fox. She is the only one who answers my "hoo-hoo-hoo." Hoo-hoo-hoo.

We call to each other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" when she hears me. We do this all night, sometimes in the dark, sometimes when we are far apart. It is how we find each other in the woods. We call when we are hunting, when we are resting, when we are scared. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We do it at dusk and again at dawn. Sometimes in the night if we are apart. The calls are soft and slow, like a conversation. She is always listening.

A stream. It runs through the meadow and under the hawthorn. I drink from it. The stream is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from the hollow. The meadow is behind it, with meadow mice. The lane is on the other side, with the barn and the shed. The lane is where the lights come from. I do not like the lights.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch over the water and let the rain drip into my mouth. Sometimes I catch a frog or a shrew and drink from the puddles after. The stream is my drink. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs through the meadow, and I hear it all night. It gurgles and splashes, and sometimes the water is still. I can tell if it's raining or if the water is low. The stream is my food, and I listen for the frogs and shrews that come to drink. I hear them splash in the water, and I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear the water moving, the stones clinking, the frogs splashing in. Sometimes I hear the water at night, when the frogs come to drink. I can tell the stream is near by the sound, and I know the frogs are there too. I don't go to the stream, but I can hear it. A stream. It runs past the wood and under the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water lapping and the frogs splashing.

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is all grass and a few scattered trees, and it is where the frogs are. I can hear them in the dark, scuttling through the long grass. The meadow is wide and the wind moves through it, carrying the smell of damp earth and the sound of crickets. I do not like it much, but I must fly over it to reach the wood. I fly out from the oak hollow, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my territory. The light fades, and I move through the meadow, the lane, the stream. I listen for the rustle of a mouse in the grass, the splash of a frog in the water. I hover, I dive, I strike. The meadow is my hunting ground. I come back to the oak when the stars come out.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and full of frogs. The frogs are not like the ones in the wood, they are bigger and jump more. I do not go there often, but sometimes I hear them from the trees. The meadow is also where the road goes, and the lights come from there. I do not like the lights. They make me nervous.

The wood is the edge of the meadow, where the stream runs. I sit on the bank and listen for the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a mouse, the flutter of a frog. The meadow is wide and open, and I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are, and the owls are me.

The meadow is where the frogs are. It is wide and soft, and the frogs come out at dusk. I sit on the edge of the wood, on the old oak, and wait. The wind moves the grass, and the frogs move with it. I hear them, and I drop. The grass is green and wet, and the frogs are brown and quick. I catch them and eat them. That is the meadow. It is where I live. Hoo... hoo
Mice. I eat them. I eat shrews, voles, frogs, worms, beetles, slugs, moths, crickets, and the occasional frog. Mice are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, and I wait. Hoot, hoot, hoo.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are the most common, and they keep me fed through the long, cold nights. I don't like frogs, they are too slippery and make too much noise. I prefer the quiet hunt of a shrew, the soft crunch of their bones under my beak.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the surface. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is good cover, but I can see through it with my eyes. I don't like the long grass much—it's too thick and makes it hard to land quietly. I prefer the meadow and the edge of the wood.

I swallow whole what I catch. A frog, a shrew, a mouse, a frog's egg, a slug, a beetle. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole and whole. The bones go down, the skin, the meat, the guts. I can feel it in my throat. It's a tight fit, but I do it. I have to. I'm a tawny owl. I don't have time to chew. I have to eat

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, scurrying through the grass. I drop from the oak, and they run. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are small, but they fill me. I eat them every night.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The oak is hollow, the stream is cold, and the wind comes through the branches. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers in the hollow. I sleep there, and I watch the stream.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it all night, listening to the wind and the water. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it. I have been here for many years, and the wood is my world.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have a nest of leaves and moss inside. I sleep there, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree. The hollow is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must. I am safe here, and I am not afraid.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and I have been there since I was a fledgling. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow is just beyond the trees. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I have raised three young there, and they have all left. I am old now, and I stay here, waiting for the night to come. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A hollow in the old oak. I have been there since I was a fledgling. It is high, safe, and warm. I have a mate who keeps it clean. We both call it home. The hollow is where I raise my young, and where I rest when the wind is too strong. It is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must.
